sentences.text: Liopleurodon was a large carnivorous marine reptile belonging to the short-necked plesiosaur clade Pliosauroidea.
This animal possessed four flippers, a short tail, a long head, and a short neck, traits typical of pliosaurids.
The largest known skull of L. ferox measures 1.54 meters in length.
An exceptionally well-preserved skeleton measuring about 4.5 meters long is exhibited at the University of Tübingen in Germany.
A partial jaw measuring 2.8 meters long is exhibited at the University of Oxford's Natural History Museum, estimated to have a total length of over 3 meters.
In 1999, a BBC documentary depicted the creature as a 25-meter-long animal, a size exaggeration that has since been corrected.
The genus Liopleurodon was first described by Henri Émile Sauvage in 1873.
Hermann Linder described specimens of Liopleurodon ferox in 1913.
Because the holotype of L. ferox is a single tooth with questionable features, recent studies recommend designating a neotype to preserve the species' validity.
Studies indicate Liopleurodon was an ambush predator that fed on fish, cephalopods, and other marine reptiles.
Studies using swimming robots suggest that Liopleurodon's flipper-based propulsion provided good acceleration, a desirable trait for an ambush predator.
Studies of the skull suggest Liopleurodon could scan the water with its nostrils to locate the source of smells.
There are currently only two known examples of Liopleurodon preserved with stomach contents.
One Liopleurodon specimen preserved stomach contents including at least seven gastroliths, numerous cephalopod hooklets, fish bones, and a reptile tooth.
Gastroliths found in Liopleurodon may have been swallowed accidentally or represent acid-resistant residue of carbonate-cemented sandstone.
Estimates suggest the holotype tooth of Liopleurodon ferox belonged to an individual approximately 5.24 meters in total length.
Liopleurodon was one of the superpredators of the Middle and Late Jurassic seas covering Europe.
The type species of the genus Liopleurodon is Liopleurodon ferox.
In 1960, Lambert Beverly Halstead considered Liopleurodon distinct from Pliosaurus based on major differences in their mandibles.
Sauvage did not assign the genus Liopleurodon to any specific reptile group when he established it in 1873.
While some studies recognize L. pachydeirus, it is generally considered a junior synonym of L. ferox due to a lack of clear diagnostic features.
In 2018, Davide Foffa and colleagues considered L. grossouvrei to potentially be a distinct genus based on its differences from P. andrewsi and L. ferox.
Liopleurodon fossils date from the Middle Jurassic to the Late Jurassic, specifically from the Callovian to the Kimmeridgian stages.
Liopleurodon lived from the Callovian stage of the Middle Jurassic to the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 166 to 155 million years ago.
Liopleurodon fossils are primarily found in Middle Jurassic deposits from Germany, England, France, and Russia.
